Target audience: Undergraduate science students or advanced high school students

Section: section_1 — The Classical vs. Quantum World (0:00-0:45)

Lecture lines:
Classical objects exist in definite, singular states.
Quantum systems allow for multiple states simultaneously.
State vectors represent these quantum states mathematically.

Planned animations:
Show a classical ball on a table (#FFFFFF).
Show a wave pattern ripple (#00FF00) representing quantum state.
Simultaneously display the ball and the wave to contrast.

Section: section_2 — Defining Superposition (0:45-2:00)

Lecture lines:
Superposition follows the linear combination principle.
Alpha and beta scale the basic states.
These act as complex probability amplitudes.
Think of them as spinning circular phasors.
Together they form a simultaneous quantum existence.

Planned animations:
Display state vector symbol |ψ> in blue (#0000FF).
Animate state 0 (#FFFF00) and state 1 (#FF0000) labels.
Display linear combination: α|0> + β|1> (#FFFFFF).

Section: section_3 — The Measurement Problem & Collapse (2:00-3:30)

Lecture lines:
Measurement forces a collapse into single states.
Born rule defines the probability of outcomes.
Square the amplitudes to find the probability.
Think of this as a shrinking cloud.
The interaction picks one definite reality.

Planned animations:
Draw a fuzzy state cloud representing superposition (#FF00FF).
Show an eye icon labeled 'Measure' (#FFFFFF).
Animate the cloud collapsing to a sharp point (#00FFFF).

Section: section_4 — Visualization: The Bloch Sphere (3:30-4:30)

Lecture lines:
Bloch spheres map all possible qubit states.
North pole represents our zero state.
South pole represents our one state.
The surface shows all possible superpositions.
Rotation traces the path between states.

Planned animations:
Draw a sphere outline in white (#FFFFFF).
Draw an arrow from center to surface (#00FF00).
Rotate the arrow to show state changes.
Label north pole as |0> and south as |1>.
Highlight the vector position on the surface.

Section: section_5 — Summary & Real-World Impact (4:30-5:00)

Lecture lines:
Superposition enables massive parallel processing power.
Quantum algorithms explore all paths simultaneously.
This shifts our logic beyond binary.

Planned animations:
List three main topics covered in text (#FFFFFF).
Animate a checkbox appearing next to each point.
Highlight the final takeaway text in gold (#FFD700).

        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

        return mobject

import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]

        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
